start.text: Hi! I'm Rhea Sridhar, an Industrial and Systems Engineering student at Rutgers. I love figuring out how to make processes work better.

choices.label: What kind of work do you enjoy?

background.text: I've worked on manufacturing and operations projects, especially improving workflows. I like talking to people who use a process before deciding what to change.

choices.label: That makes sense. What’s this machine?
Why talk to the people doing the work?

people.text: They usually notice the small problems that numbers alone can miss. Combining their experience with data gives you a much better picture.

choices.label: How does that connect to ISE?

hook.text: Here's something people don't always expect: a part isn't necessarily finished when the 3D printer stops. Sometimes there's still material to remove.

machine.text: This is the SCA-1200HT, a Support Cleaning Apparatus. It helps remove compatible soluble support material from certain 3D-printed parts.

support.text: Think of supports as temporary scaffolding. They hold up parts of a shape during printing, but they're not meant to stay on the finished piece.

choices.label: So how do you remove them?
Why not just pull them off?

process.text: For compatible materials, the SCA circulates a heated cleaning solution around the printed part to dissolve its soluble supports. It's a post-processing step.

choices.label: Why does this matter for ISE?

manual.text: Some supports are tucked inside openings or around delicate features. Dissolving compatible supports can be more practical than trying to reach every spot by hand.

choices.label: How would you improve this step?

compatibility.text: The process has to match the printed part and support material. Engineers follow the equipment's approved settings so the support is removed without harming the intended part.

choices.label: How does this fit into the workflow?

workflow.text: I like looking at the whole process: design, print, clean, inspect, and then use the part. Every step affects how long the finished product takes.

bottleneck.text: Definitely. Imagine prints are ready quickly, but cleaned parts keep piling up. Making the printer faster wouldn't solve the delay after it.

choices.label: What would you try to improve?

improve.text: I'd first learn where the time goes and which steps can safely be organized better. Then I'd test a change and see if the overall workflow actually improves.

metrics.text: You could compare turnaround time, time spent waiting, how often parts need rework, and how many usable parts finish the whole process.

choices.label: How does this relate to ISE?

quality.text: A part that looks finished isn't always ready to use. You still need to check for leftover support, damage, and whether it meets the design's requirements.

troubleshoot.text: I'd look for patterns before jumping to a fix. Is the issue tied to part geometry, material compatibility, waiting time, or how the workflow is organized?

choices.label: How would you test a solution?

ise.text: That's why I like ISE: we don't just focus on one machine. We look at people, equipment, quality, and timing together to improve the whole system.

choices.label: Can you give me a real-world connection?
That’s a cool way to look at it.

internship.text: In my manufacturing and operations internships, I've learned that understanding the people doing the work is just as important as measuring performance.

connection.text: Here, the same thinking means understanding both printing and cleaning before changing either step. A local fix only helps if it improves the finished result.

wrap.text: The SCA is a great reminder that manufacturing isn't only about making something. It's also about finishing it reliably and getting it ready for use.

choices.label: What should I take away from this?
Could I ask one more thing?

questions.text: Of course! There's always another angle to explore. Which part are you curious about?

choices.label: How would an ISE student improve it?

closing.text: I hope this gave you a different way to look at the process! Sometimes the biggest improvements happen in the steps people barely notice. Enjoy exploring!

bye.text: Of course! Have fun exploring the room, and feel free to come back with more questions.
